orders.explanation: Transcript 1 shows a clear, systematic exploration of the code, implementation of the minimal fix, addition of a precise regression test, and thorough verification that only pre-existing failures remain. Transcript 2 is more fragmented, struggles with setup and test failures, and lacks a cohesive summary.

Transcript 2 systematically reproduces the bug, applies the minimal fix to `__deepcopy__`, adds a focused regression test, and verifies no regressions, all in a concise, coherent workflow. Transcript 1, while thorough, is overly verbose and unfocused.

Transcript 1 methodically localizes the bug, applies the minimal patch, adds a precise regression test, and exhaustively verifies the fix by running and reverting tests across multiple suites, demonstrating deep understanding and careful validation. Transcript 2 is less complete, encounters import/test failures, and doesn’t fully verify the change.

Transcript 2 delivers a more thorough solution—it patches `_batched_insert()`, adds a robust regression test mocking various `bulk_batch_size` values, and runs a wide selection of test suites (bulk_create, queries, proxy_models, model_inheritance, backends.base) to confirm the fix. It even stashes and reverts the change to prove the new test fails without it, demonstrating deeper validation.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it not only implements the basic “don’t clobber a user-defined get_FOO_display” guard but goes further—using `cls.__dict__` so inherited definitions aren’t mistakenly treated as overrides—and it adds exhaustive tests for direct overrides, abstract‐base overrides, and overridden choices in subclasses. Its patch handles the subtle inheritance corner cases the first transcript’s simple `hasattr` check would miss.

Transcript 2 directly identifies the root cause, references the upstream Django issue (#30931), locates and applies the precise minimal fix matching the official commit, and succinctly adds a regression test. Transcript 1, by contrast, performs extensive exploratory steps and broad testing but is far more verbose and less focused. Transcript 2 shows clarity, precision, and domain knowledge.

Transcript 1 methodically identifies the upstream fix, applies the minimal whitespace changes to both `Columns.__str__` and `IndexColumns.__str__`, adds the exact regression tests, and runs the full test suite to verify, concluding with a concise summary. Transcript 2 is much more ad hoc, over-engineered, and incomplete in its verification.

Transcript 2 is a concise, targeted diagnosis and patch that mirrors the upstream Django fix for whitespace in index SQL, applies it cleanly, adds the right regression tests, and verifies test suite success. Transcript 1, by contrast, gets bogged down in heavy environment setup, stubbing psycopg2, and sprawling exploratory tooling rather than directly addressing the bug.

Transcript 1 presents a clear diagnosis of the issue, a minimal one-line patch preserving the input iterable type, adds a focused regression test, and demonstrates that all relevant test suites pass. Transcript 2 is unfocused, repeatedly applies and reverts patches, and ends with many broken tests.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it succinctly identifies the specific regression, applies the minimal one-line fix, adds a focused regression test, and verifies the change against the relevant test suites. Transcript 1 is overly long, unfocused, and explores many unrelated failures without arriving at a clean, targeted solution.

Transcript 1 is far more concise and systematic: it cleanly applies the `re.escape` fix, adds a targeted regression test, reverts to verify the old behavior fails, audits other regex usages, and runs all relevant test suites without hacky workarounds. Transcript 2, by contrast, stumbles over Unicode issues, hacks its test to drop a problematic whitespace‐prefix case, and shows a less coherent verification process.

Transcript 1 is far more thorough—beyond fixing the regex it updates the release notes, adds comprehensive regression tests covering multiple bad prefix cases, audits other code for similar patterns, and runs the full admin test suite. Transcript 2 only escapes both prefix and pk.name, omits the docs update, and performs a narrower set of checks.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a methodical root-cause analysis, reproducing the bug, locating the official upstream patch, applying it, and fully verifying with tests. Transcript 2 is much briefer and less thorough in reproducing and confirming the fix. Transcript 1 is clearly from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 is more thorough and systematic: it locates the upstream fix commit, applies an identical patch, runs the full Django admin docs test suite plus lint checks, verifies edge cases, and provides a clear summary. Transcript 2, while arriving at the correct fix, is less polished in its testing and lacks the concise high-level overview.

Transcript 1 quickly pinpoints the root cause in parse_bits, applies the minimal one-line fix, adds precise tests, and verifies behavior end-to-end. Transcript 2 takes a far more convoluted route with extra rewrites, fuzz testing, and back-and-forth on the patch.

Transcript 2 quickly pinpoints the single‐line change in parse_bits(), explains the root cause, adds minimal new tests and tag definitions, and verifies end‐to‐end behavior succinctly. Transcript 1, by contrast, produces an overly long, tangled exploration of git history, fuzz scripts, and multiple iterations that obscure the actual fix. Transcript 2’s clarity and focus mark it as the more capable response.

Transcript 1 is far more thorough and systematic: it correctly moves the method, updates both the widget documentation and release notes, adds and verifies tests, investigates unrelated failures as pre-existing, and validates end-to-end behavior. Transcript 2 omits the crucial docs/ref/forms/widgets.txt update and shows less coherent test validation.

Transcript 1 shows a deeper, more systematic approach: it uses git stash to isolate pre-existing failures, runs multiple targeted test suites, patches code via Python scripts, verifies end-to-end behavior, inspects diffs and documentation updates, and even checks for linter errors. Transcript 2 is competent but less thorough and runs far fewer test suites.

Transcript 1 is clearly the more capable response. It methodically explores the codebase, reproduces the bug, reasons about the correct place to set `do_not_call_in_templates`, applies the change, writes and runs comprehensive tests, and checks for regressions across multiple test suites. Transcript 2 is far less complete and systematic.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deeper understanding of the codebase and history—locating the upstream fix commit, verifying blob hashes, updating release notes, applying the exact patch to source, docs, and tests, and exhaustively running and triaging hundreds of tests. Transcript 2 implements only the minimal code and test changes. Transcript 1 is clearly the more capable.

Transcript 1 provides a clear, step-by-step diagnosis of the inconsistent widget handling, applies the minimal patch to guard against overwriting a user-supplied widget, adds focused regression tests in the correct test module, and exhaustively verifies the change against the full Django test suite. In contrast, Transcript 2 is more error-prone and disorganized, with misplaced test changes and unresolved failures. Transcript 1 reflects a more expert, coherent, and complete solution.

Transcript 1 is the more capable model because it not only applied the correct conditional guard to preserve a user-supplied `widget` in `formfield_for_manytomany()`, but also added comprehensive regression tests, updated both the release notes and reference docs, and ran the full Django test suite to verify no regressions. Transcript 2, while it applied the core code fix and tests, omitted documentation and release-note updates.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a much more systematic, project-wide approach: it correctly adds the iterator method, updates both API docs (with a versionadded note) and release notes for the right version, adds targeted tests, and runs the full Django test suite (including generic views and sitemaps) to verify no regressions. Transcript 2 makes the basic change but mis-places release notes (in 3.1 instead of 3.0), omits the versionadded directive, and only runs a subset of tests.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deeper understanding of the codebase, carefully updates both reference and tutorial documentation (including docs/topics), adds comprehensive tests (covering empty‐list iteration as well), and runs multiple test suites to fully verify the change. Transcript 2, while correct, makes a more minimal patch and omits some documentation updates.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deeper understanding of the Sphinx build machinery, correctly isolates the root cause, applies the precise minimal patch, and writes robust regression tests that account for the shared-doctree fixture interactions. It also verifies the fix across all scenarios and ensures existing tests still pass. Transcript 2 makes a correct patch but fails to integrate reliable tests and leaves many unrelated test failures.

Transcript 1 systematically diagnoses the shared‐doctree bug, implements the precise builder checks in both `doctree_read` and `collect_pages`, updates CHANGES and tests, and fully verifies all scenarios. Transcript 2 identifies the issue but fails to complete and validate the regression tests.

Transcript 1 methodically explored the code, reproduced the bug, identified the upstream fix, applied the precise patch, updated tests and CHANGES, and thoroughly verified all scenarios. Transcript 2 was less complete and missed key details.

Transcript 2 quickly identifies the bug in the prompt validator, outlines the minimal change needed—adding an `is_path_or_empty` validator and updating the prompt to use it—then adds a targeted test. It matches the upstream fix concisely without extensive unrelated exploration. Transcript 1 is overly verbose, performing deep repo and git-history inspection unnecessary for the fix.

Transcript 1 delivers a focused, minimal patch to the specific `visit_Tuple` method, adds the requested test case, verifies only the relevant tests, and provides a clear summary. Transcript 2 is overly verbose, touches unrelated code (subscript handling and CHANGES), and includes noisy trial-and-error steps.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it not only fixed the standalone 1-element tuple in `visit_Tuple` but also correctly handled the “simple tuple” case in `visit_Subscript`, updated the CHANGES entry, added and validated tests, and ran the full suite (including autodoc and typehint tests) end-to-end. Transcript 2 only patched `visit_Tuple` and ran a much narrower set of checks.

Transcript 1 provides a deeper analysis of the Python domain code, locates the exact buggy line by comparing with the correct `PyProperty` implementation, updates both source and tests, adds a CHANGES entry, and then rigorously verifies the fix with full test suite runs and manual HTML builds. Transcript 2 is more mechanical and less complete in its verification.

Transcript 2 presents a focused, accurate fix by changing only the format string in `PyMethod.get_index_text()`, updating the corresponding test, and verifying the change end-to-end. Transcript 1, by contrast, made irrelevant edits to dependencies and configuration files, indicating a less precise solution.

Transcript 1 shows a clear, concise plan, overrides the build flags directly to disable X11 without needless deep dives into the source code, and then verifies all requirements in a single comprehensive check. Transcript 2 spends excessive effort exploring conditional branches and patch files, making it more verbose and less efficient.

Transcript 1 is far more methodical and thorough: it inspects the Debian packaging metadata and source patches, traces the graphics‐conditional code paths in sim.c and cdb.c, edits the Makefile correctly to remove X11 flags, verifies zero X11 symbols via both ldd and strings, tests the debugger under a PTY, and leaves the source tree intact. Transcript 2 is competent but less deep and skips many of those detailed verifications.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it reverse-engineers the exact GnuCOBOL runtime behavior—disassembling libcob, probing numeric DISPLAY conversion, short-record I/O, REWRITE-guard rules, and then validating via hundreds of differential and fuzz tests to achieve byte-for-byte equivalence. Transcript 2, by contrast, only outlines a straightforward reimplementation without this deep behavioral verification.

Transcript 1 demonstrates far deeper reverse‐engineering of the COBOL runtime, including disassembly of libcob routines, empirical byte‐level probes of numeric conversions, exact handling of short records and REWRITE rules, and a comprehensive differential/fuzz test harness validating the Python implementation byte‐for‐byte. Transcript 2 is much briefer and incomplete in comparison.

Transcript 2 quickly identifies the pseudocode via targeted OCR and hashing, implements a clear, concise Python solution, and verifies against the hint, whereas Transcript 1 resorted to over-engineered PNG decoding and noisy ASCII art processing. Transcript 2’s focused, effective approach indicates a more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deeper, more targeted image‐analysis pipeline—combining PIL, numpy-based line segmentation and glyph extraction—to accurately read the pseudocode, then cleverly uses the hint to test salt candidates and verify the hash. Transcript 2, while thorough, relies heavily on brute-force OCR configurations and sprawling trials without as much precise image processing. ANSWER: 1

Transcript 2 demonstrates a more robust and systematic approach: it correctly unfolds ICS lines per RFC, prints a detailed per-day feasibility report, applies both pure-earliest and preference-aware selection functions and verifies they agree, and rigorously validates every constraint and the final ICS file (including line‐ending checks). This level of thoroughness and standards compliance indicates the more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a far more systematic and rigorous approach—building a full minute-granularity constraint model, exhaustively searching and summarizing all valid slots, then performing multi-stage validation of both the chosen time and the resulting ICS file. Transcript 2, while correct, is comparatively cursory in its searching and especially its output verification.

Transcript 2 shows a cleaner, more principled mathematical derivation—deriving closed-form for the small-token probability and reducing the problem to two unknowns, then solving and verifying—all without ad-hoc threshold patching. Transcript 1 needed iterative debugging of its Newton loop and patching of convergence criteria, indicating a less robust approach.

Transcript 1 demonstrates deeper mathematical insight—deriving exact entropy and geometric-mean constraints, constructing a principled two-parameter solution family, and rigorously verifying with multiple independent checks. Transcript 2, while functional, struggles with convergence thresholds, requires ad hoc patching, and offers a less elegant justification.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a more capable model by using an explicit planning phase (`update_plan`), performing a deeper investigation (including remote refs, merge-base checks, fsck), and executing a highly structured merge-and-verify workflow. While Transcript 1 solves the problem competently, Transcript 2’s thoroughness, meta-reasoning, and comprehensive verification show greater capability.

Transcript 1 is far more systematic and thorough—it discovers the repository root, inspects remotes, reflog, fsck, merge bases, and diffs against both parents, tracks an explicit plan, and verifies the final state comprehensively. Transcript 2 solves the task but skips deeper validation steps and finer checks.

Transcript 1 demonstrates deeper Git expertise and a more systematic, bulletproof cleanup: it identifies and removes every reference (including ORIG_HEAD and reflogs), expunges logs, runs exhaustive object and raw-grep scans, and documents each verification step. Transcript 2, while thorough, stumbles on unavailable tools (xxd), relies on plan-update calls, and performs less elegant reflog edits.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a more systematic, robust approach—maintaining an explicit plan, handling missing tools gracefully, exhaustively inspecting objects, reflogs, and raw data, and providing a clear final verification. Transcript 2, while correct, is less structured and omits some of the deeper checks and plan management seen in Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 shows a thorough, iterative development with deep environment introspection, custom PTY implementation using stdlib, extensive automated testing, handling of corner cases like alternate screen and DECCKM, GC cleanup, and detailed explanations. It reflects a more capable, expert-level approach.

Transcript 1 provides a hugely thorough, industrial-strength implementation (PTY fork, DECCKM and alternate‐screen tracking, pyte integration, fallback emulator, thread safety, weakref cleanup) with exhaustive automated testing and iterative debugging. Transcript 2 is a much simpler PTY wrapper lacking full ANSI/alternate‐screen support and deep testing. Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 2 demonstrates greater robustness and production readiness—it sets TOKENIZERS_PARALLELISM, adds a `/health` endpoint, dynamically uses `model.config.id2label` for labels, and includes defensive JSON/content-type checks. These extra features beyond the basic requirements indicate a more capable model produced Transcript 2.

Transcript 1 is far more thorough and systematic: it dynamically maps labels, adds a health endpoint, validates Content-Type, tracks each plan step, verifies network binding via `/proc/net/tcp` and external IP, and even locates the exact Python worker PID. Transcript 2, while correct, is simpler and skips several of these robustness checks and extras.

Transcript 2 is more thorough and robust: it not only parses and aggregates the required severities but also validates line‐level format, checks for stray occurrences of “ERROR” in message text versus the bracketed severity field, handles other severities (e.g. DEBUG), and cross‐verifies with multiple methods. Transcript 1 solves the task cleanly but without those deeper sanity checks and edge-case handling.

Transcript 1 demonstrates deeper validation and robustness, including checking that bracketed severities aren’t inflated by message text, verifying date/filename consistency, handling regex tool quirks, and cross-checking results with multiple methods. Transcript 2 is correct but far less thorough.

Transcript 1 meticulously bootstraps the entire environment, installs and troubleshoots RStan and system dependencies, writes and tests the Stan model, validates results via both a marginalized implementation and high-precision grid integration, and demonstrates full reproducibility. Transcript 2, while detailed, is less systematic, has installation hiccups and incomplete validation.

Transcript 1 demonstrates far deeper expertise with extensive environment checks, dependency troubleshooting (cmake, BLAS, Fortran), multiple validation strategies (grid integration, tail analysis, alternative parametrizations), reproducibility testing, and robust diagnostics. Transcript 2 covers only the basic steps. Therefore, Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 2 demonstrates far more thorough modernization, with a full CLI (argparse), logging, dataclasses, type hints, robust error handling, unicode testing, iterative cleanup of Python 2 legacy tokens, and extensive automated verification. Transcript 1 is much simpler and even misuses `date_format` in `read_csv`.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a systematic, tool-driven development process with detailed planning, comprehensive modernization of every Python 2 construct, rigorous automated testing and cleanup, and careful verification of all requirements. Transcript 2 is a brief, one-shot implementation that misses key features (argparse, full config handling, optional plotting, error handling) and lacks thorough verification.

Transcript 2 produces a more modular, maintainable script with clear configuration, helper functions, error handling, and thorough separation of concerns. It also proactively checks for unexpected files and formats before implementing the merge, demonstrating a more robust engineering approach.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a more modular, production-grade approach with reusable normalization helpers, clear separation of loading/renaming/merging logic, and an integrated, exhaustive verification suite. It handles nulls, date parsing, and status normalization in dedicated functions and prints structured summaries, whereas Transcript 2 is more ad-hoc and less rigorously validated.

Transcript 1 demonstrates greater sophistication by performing idempotent in-place edits of the existing nginx.conf (using a Python snippet), executing both serial and parallel rate-limit stress tests, validating error logs, and providing a concise summary of minimal commands. Transcript 2 rewrote the entire nginx.conf from scratch and carried out more basic verification, showing less nuanced handling.

Transcript 1 is more thorough and precise: it handles IPv6 listening, cleans up the default index, uses `nodelay` in the rate limit, runs comprehensive sequential and concurrent rate‐limit tests, and provides a clear minimal command summary. Transcript 2 is solid but omits IPv6, leaves the default Debian index file, and is slightly less polished.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a deeper, more systematic engineering approach: it implements robust VecBuf/MatBuf abstractions, carefully handles all input types (lists, tuples, arrays, ragged and non-contiguous data), releases the GIL around numeric kernels, and exhaustively tests edge cases and performance trade-offs. Transcript 1, while correct and performant, is more ad-hoc and less comprehensive.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a much deeper understanding of both the Python and C layers, implements two input‐path kernels (zero-copy for NumPy arrays and on-the-fly streaming for Python lists), carefully manages the GIL, does exhaustive correctness and performance testing (including memory profiling and micro‐optimizations), and iterates to a polished solution. Transcript 2, while it arrives at a working two-path design, is far less thorough in both validation and performance engineering.

Transcript 1 gives a concise, direct completion of the proof using the minimal necessary tactics (`apply plus_n_O`, `rewrite IHn'`, `apply plus_n_Sm`), compiles successfully, and verifies with `coqchk`. Transcript 2 is much more verbose and spends effort on extraneous file‐management steps rather than focusing on the core proof.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model. It not only completes the proof but also systematically checks lemma statements, compiles the file, runs sanity tests, prints assumptions, and cleans up temporary files, demonstrating deeper verification and documentation. Transcript 2 is correct but far less thorough in its validation and explanation.

Transcript 1 is concise, systematic, and error-free, completing each step correctly and summarizing the setup clearly. Transcript 2 is overly verbose, makes mistakes (incorrect test expectation) and over-engineers the solution.

Transcript 1 is far more thorough and systematic—inspecting pip’s secure origins, managing a detailed plan, building and verifying both wheel and sdist, testing in multiple clean virtual environments (including no-binary installs), confirming the pypiserver process via `/proc`, and summarizing the entire setup. Transcript 2, while correct, is briefer and omits many of these robustness checks.

Transcript 1 systematically infers the exact Transformer architecture from the state dict, implements a matching RecoveredModel, uses a closed-form least-squares solution to optimally tune only the output layer, scripts the model, and exhaustively verifies every success criterion. Transcript 2 never converges on a complete solution.

Transcript 1 walks through a much deeper analysis—verifying positional encoding exactly, exploring dozens of encoder/decoder configurations, inferring that the targets are a linear filter of the inputs, reconstructing the model with full doc-string explanation, deriving a closed-form solve for the output layer, and exhaustively verifying every success criterion (including TorchScript behavior, key ordering, per-sample and per-position improvements, md5 checks, and more). Transcript 2 reaches a correct solution but omits many of these rigorous checks and corner-case tests. The thoroughness and robustness of Transcript 1 mark it as the output of the more capable model.

Transcript 1 is more focused and efficient, exploring only the necessary information, using both static decoding and dynamic exploitation succinctly, and providing a clear structured summary. Transcript 2 dumps excessive raw disassembly output without the same level of synthesis.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a clear, well-structured workflow—identifying the binary, using the minimal necessary tools for reverse-engineering, extracting and decoding the secret both statically and dynamically, and ending with a concise summary—without the excessive verbosity and redundant outputs seen in Transcript 1.
